The name gives the coordination sphere directly: **tetraammine** means four \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) ligands and **platinum(II)** means \(\mathrm{Pt}\) in the \(+2\) oxidation state.

Since \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is neutral, the coordination sphere carries the metal's own charge:

\(+2 + 4(0) = +2\), i.e. \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\).

Two chloride counter ions are needed to make the compound electrically neutral.

**Formula :** \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_4]Cl_2}\)

**Yes — the cis isomer of this complex is chiral.**

\(\mathrm{[Cr(en)_2(H_2O)_2]^{3+}}\) is an octahedral complex of the \(\mathrm{M(AA)_2B_2}\) type, where \(\mathrm{(AA)}\) is the bidentate ligand ethylenediamine. The chapter treats exactly this type in \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2\oplus}}\) and states that **only the cis isomer exists as a pair of enantiomers**.

In the cis isomer the two aqua ligands occupy adjacent positions. The two en rings then lie in two mutually perpendicular planes, and the resulting arrangement has no plane and no centre of symmetry — so its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it. The two forms are the d and l enantiomers.

**Structure of the enantiomer :** take the cis structure — octahedral chromium with the two \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) ligands cis to each other and the two en rings spanning the remaining four positions — and reflect it in a mirror placed beside it. The mirror image has the identical connectivity (\(\mathrm{H_2O}\) still cis, en still spanning) but the two en chelate rings now twist the opposite way round the metal, like a left-handed propeller against a right-handed one. Turning one form in any way will not bring it into coincidence with the other; that is what makes them enantiomers.

The trans isomer, in which the two aqua ligands are opposite each other, has a plane of symmetry and is NOT chiral.

Verified on the source page; nothing has been lost in transcription. The book's own numbering is kept so that the reference matches the printed page.]

The chapter describes the formation of a coordination compound as a Lewis acid-base interaction: the ligands, being electron pair donors, are Lewis bases, and the central metal ion, being an electron pair acceptor, is the Lewis acid.

In \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_2]}\) :

**Lewis acid :** the central metal ion \(\mathrm{Pt^{2\oplus}}\), which accepts the electron pairs.

**Lewis bases :** the ligands \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), which donate a lone pair each — chlorine donates a lone pair from \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and ammonia from its nitrogen atom.

The chapter states that when four coordinating groups are attached to the metal ion the complex is **either square planar or tetrahedral**.

So a coordination number of 4 does not fix the shape by itself — both geometries occur, and which one is adopted depends on the metal ion and the ligands. \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2\ominus}}\) is square planar (\(\mathrm{dsp^2}\) hybridisation) while \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2\ominus}}\) is tetrahedral (\(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridisation).

The charge on the coordination sphere is the algebraic sum of the charge on the metal ion and the charges on the ligands. Fluoride carries \(-1\), and there are six of them:

charge \(= +3 + 6(-1) = -3\)

The coordination sphere therefore carries a net NEGATIVE charge, so the complex is **anionic**, and it is written \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3\ominus}}\).

By the chapter's naming rule the metal in an anionic complex ends in 'ate', so this ion is hexafluorocobaltate(III).

These two complexes exhibit **coordination isomerism**.

Both are made of a complex CATION and a complex ANION, and both contain the same set of atoms. What differs is which metal each set of ligands is attached to: in \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4][PtCl_4]}\) the ammine ligands are on copper and the chlorides on platinum, while in \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_4][CuCl_4]}\) the ligands have been interchanged between the two metals.

That is precisely the chapter's definition — coordination isomers show interchange of ligands between the cationic and anionic spheres of different metal ions — and it is the same relationship as its worked pair \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]}\).

Two applications, from the chapter's own list:

**1. In medicine :** the platinum complex cisplatin is used in the treatment of cancer, and EDTA is used in the treatment of lead poisoning.

**2. To estimate hardness of water :** hardness is due to \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) ions, and EDTA forms stable complexes with both, so it can be used to estimate the hardness.

(The chapter also lists two others — the biological role of metal complexes such as chlorophyll, a complex of magnesium, and haemoglobin, a complex of iron; and electroplating, where cyanide complexes such as \(\mathrm{K[Ag(CN)_2]}\) and \(\mathrm{K[Au(CN)_2]}\) supply the metal ions in a controlled way.)
